problem_description.description: The leader of some very secretive organization has decided to invite all other members to a meeting. All members of the organization live in the same town which can be represented as $$$n$$$ crossroads connected by $$$m$$$ two-directional streets. The meeting will be held in the leader's house near the crossroad $$$1$$$. There are $$$k$$$ members of the organization invited to the meeting; $$$i$$$-th of them lives near the crossroad $$$a_i$$$. All members of the organization receive the message about the meeting at the same moment and start moving to the location where the meeting is held. In the beginning of each minute each person is located at some crossroad. He or she can either wait a minute at this crossroad, or spend a minute to walk from the current crossroad along some street to another crossroad (obviously, it is possible to start walking along the street only if it begins or ends at the current crossroad). In the beginning of the first minute each person is at the crossroad where he or she lives. As soon as a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, he or she immediately comes to the leader's house and attends the meeting.Obviously, the leader wants all other members of the organization to come up as early as possible. But, since the organization is very secretive, the leader does not want to attract much attention. Let's denote the discontent of the leader as follows  initially the discontent is $$$0$$$;  whenever a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, the discontent of the leader increases by $$$c \cdot x$$$, where $$$c$$$ is some fixed constant, and $$$x$$$ is the number of minutes it took the person to reach the crossroad number $$$1$$$;  whenever $$$x$$$ members of the organization walk along the same street at the same moment in the same direction, $$$dx^2$$$ is added to the discontent, where $$$d$$$ is some fixed constant. This is not cumulative: for example, if two persons are walking along the same street in the same direction at the same moment, then $$$4d$$$ is added to the discontent, not $$$5d$$$. Before sending a message about the meeting, the leader can tell each member of the organization which path they should choose and where they should wait. Help the leader to establish a plan for every member of the organization so they all reach the crossroad $$$1$$$, and the discontent is minimized.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains five integer numbers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, $$$k$$$, $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 50$$$, $$$n - 1 \le m \le 50$$$, $$$1 \le k, c, d \le 50$$$) — the number of crossroads, the number of streets, the number of persons invited to the meeting and the constants affecting the discontent, respectively. The second line contains $$$k$$$ numbers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_k$$$ ($$$2 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the crossroads where the members of the organization live. Then $$$m$$$ lines follow, each denoting a bidirectional street. Each line contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i, y_i \le n$$$, $$$x_i \ne y_i$$$) denoting a street connecting crossroads $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$. There may be multiple streets connecting the same pair of crossroads. It is guaranteed that every crossroad can be reached from every other crossroad using the given streets.
problem_description.output_spec: Print one integer: the minimum discontent of the leader after everyone reaches crossroad $$$1$$$.
problem_description.notes: NoteThe best course of action in the first test is the following:  the first person goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the second person waits one minute on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the third person waits two minutes on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the fourth person waits three minutes on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting.

problem_description.description: The leader of some very secretive organization has decided to invite all other members to a meeting. All members of the organization live in the same town which can be represented as $$$n$$$ crossroads connected by $$$m$$$ two-directional streets. The meeting will be held in the leader's house near the crossroad $$$1$$$. There are $$$k$$$ members of the organization invited to the meeting; $$$i$$$-th of them lives near the crossroad $$$a_i$$$. All members of the organization receive the message about the meeting at the same moment and start moving to the location where the meeting is held. In the beginning of each minute each person is located at some crossroad. He or she can either wait a minute at this crossroad, or spend a minute to walk from the current crossroad along some street to another crossroad (obviously, it is possible to start walking along the street only if it begins or ends at the current crossroad). In the beginning of the first minute each person is at the crossroad where he or she lives. As soon as a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, he or she immediately comes to the leader's house and attends the meeting.Obviously, the leader wants all other members of the organization to come up as early as possible. But, since the organization is very secretive, the leader does not want to attract much attention. Let's denote the discontent of the leader as follows  initially the discontent is $$$0$$$;  whenever a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, the discontent of the leader increases by $$$c \cdot x$$$, where $$$c$$$ is some fixed constant, and $$$x$$$ is the number of minutes it took the person to reach the crossroad number $$$1$$$;  whenever $$$x$$$ members of the organization walk along the same street at the same moment in the same direction, $$$dx^2$$$ is added to the discontent, where $$$d$$$ is some fixed constant. This is not cumulative: for example, if two persons are walking along the same street in the same direction at the same moment, then $$$4d$$$ is added to the discontent, not $$$5d$$$. Before sending a message about the meeting, the leader can tell each member of the organization which path they should choose and where they should wait. Help the leader to establish a plan for every member of the organization so they all reach the crossroad $$$1$$$, and the discontent is minimized.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains five integer numbers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, $$$k$$$, $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 50$$$, $$$n - 1 \le m \le 50$$$, $$$1 \le k, c, d \le 50$$$) — the number of crossroads, the number of streets, the number of persons invited to the meeting and the constants affecting the discontent, respectively. The second line contains $$$k$$$ numbers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_k$$$ ($$$2 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the crossroads where the members of the organization live. Then $$$m$$$ lines follow, each denoting a bidirectional street. Each line contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i, y_i \le n$$$, $$$x_i \ne y_i$$$) denoting a street connecting crossroads $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$. There may be multiple streets connecting the same pair of crossroads. It is guaranteed that every crossroad can be reached from every other crossroad using the given streets.
problem_description.output_spec: Print one integer: the minimum discontent of the leader after everyone reaches crossroad $$$1$$$.
problem_description.notes: NoteThe best course of action in the first test is the following:  the first person goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the second person waits one minute on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the third person waits two minutes on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the fourth person waits three minutes on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting.

problem_description.description: The leader of some very secretive organization has decided to invite all other members to a meeting. All members of the organization live in the same town which can be represented as $$$n$$$ crossroads connected by $$$m$$$ two-directional streets. The meeting will be held in the leader's house near the crossroad $$$1$$$. There are $$$k$$$ members of the organization invited to the meeting; $$$i$$$-th of them lives near the crossroad $$$a_i$$$. All members of the organization receive the message about the meeting at the same moment and start moving to the location where the meeting is held. In the beginning of each minute each person is located at some crossroad. He or she can either wait a minute at this crossroad, or spend a minute to walk from the current crossroad along some street to another crossroad (obviously, it is possible to start walking along the street only if it begins or ends at the current crossroad). In the beginning of the first minute each person is at the crossroad where he or she lives. As soon as a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, he or she immediately comes to the leader's house and attends the meeting.Obviously, the leader wants all other members of the organization to come up as early as possible. But, since the organization is very secretive, the leader does not want to attract much attention. Let's denote the discontent of the leader as follows  initially the discontent is $$$0$$$;  whenever a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, the discontent of the leader increases by $$$c \cdot x$$$, where $$$c$$$ is some fixed constant, and $$$x$$$ is the number of minutes it took the person to reach the crossroad number $$$1$$$;  whenever $$$x$$$ members of the organization walk along the same street at the same moment in the same direction, $$$dx^2$$$ is added to the discontent, where $$$d$$$ is some fixed constant. This is not cumulative: for example, if two persons are walking along the same street in the same direction at the same moment, then $$$4d$$$ is added to the discontent, not $$$5d$$$. Before sending a message about the meeting, the leader can tell each member of the organization which path they should choose and where they should wait. Help the leader to establish a plan for every member of the organization so they all reach the crossroad $$$1$$$, and the discontent is minimized.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains five integer numbers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, $$$k$$$, $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 50$$$, $$$n - 1 \le m \le 50$$$, $$$1 \le k, c, d \le 50$$$) — the number of crossroads, the number of streets, the number of persons invited to the meeting and the constants affecting the discontent, respectively. The second line contains $$$k$$$ numbers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_k$$$ ($$$2 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the crossroads where the members of the organization live. Then $$$m$$$ lines follow, each denoting a bidirectional street. Each line contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i, y_i \le n$$$, $$$x_i \ne y_i$$$) denoting a street connecting crossroads $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$. There may be multiple streets connecting the same pair of crossroads. It is guaranteed that every crossroad can be reached from every other crossroad using the given streets.
problem_description.output_spec: Print one integer: the minimum discontent of the leader after everyone reaches crossroad $$$1$$$.

problem_description.description: The leader of some very secretive organization has decided to invite all other members to a meeting. All members of the organization live in the same town which can be represented as $$$n$$$ crossroads connected by $$$m$$$ two-directional streets. The meeting will be held in the leader's house near the crossroad $$$1$$$. There are $$$k$$$ members of the organization invited to the meeting; $$$i$$$-th of them lives near the crossroad $$$a_i$$$. All members of the organization receive the message about the meeting at the same moment and start moving to the location where the meeting is held. In the beginning of each minute each person is located at some crossroad. He or she can either wait a minute at this crossroad, or spend a minute to walk from the current crossroad along some street to another crossroad (obviously, it is possible to start walking along the street only if it begins or ends at the current crossroad). In the beginning of the first minute each person is at the crossroad where he or she lives. As soon as a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, he or she immediately comes to the leader's house and attends the meeting.Obviously, the leader wants all other members of the organization to come up as early as possible. But, since the organization is very secretive, the leader does not want to attract much attention. Let's denote the discontent of the leader as follows  initially the discontent is $$$0$$$;  whenever a person reaches the crossroad number $$$1$$$, the discontent of the leader increases by $$$c \cdot x$$$, where $$$c$$$ is some fixed constant, and $$$x$$$ is the number of minutes it took the person to reach the crossroad number $$$1$$$;  whenever $$$x$$$ members of the organization walk along the same street at the same moment in the same direction, $$$dx^2$$$ is added to the discontent, where $$$d$$$ is some fixed constant. This is not cumulative: for example, if two persons are walking along the same street in the same direction at the same moment, then $$$4d$$$ is added to the discontent, not $$$5d$$$. Before sending a message about the meeting, the leader can tell each member of the organization which path they should choose and where they should wait. Help the leader to establish a plan for every member of the organization so they all reach the crossroad $$$1$$$, and the discontent is minimized.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains five integer numbers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, $$$k$$$, $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 50$$$, $$$n - 1 \le m \le 50$$$, $$$1 \le k, c, d \le 50$$$) — the number of crossroads, the number of streets, the number of persons invited to the meeting and the constants affecting the discontent, respectively. The second line contains $$$k$$$ numbers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_k$$$ ($$$2 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the crossroads where the members of the organization live. Then $$$m$$$ lines follow, each denoting a bidirectional street. Each line contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i, y_i \le n$$$, $$$x_i \ne y_i$$$) denoting a street connecting crossroads $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$. There may be multiple streets connecting the same pair of crossroads. It is guaranteed that every crossroad can be reached from every other crossroad using the given streets.
problem_description.output_spec: Print one integer: the minimum discontent of the leader after everyone reaches crossroad $$$1$$$.
problem_description.notes: NoteThe best course of action in the first test is the following:  the first person goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the second person waits one minute on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the third person waits two minutes on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting;  the fourth person waits three minutes on the crossroad $$$3$$$, then goes along the street $$$2$$$ to the crossroad $$$2$$$, then goes along the street $$$1$$$ to the crossroad $$$1$$$ and attends the meeting.

problem_description.description: There is the faculty of Computer Science in Berland. In the social net "TheContact!" for each course of this faculty there is the special group whose name equals the year of university entrance of corresponding course of students at the university. Each of students joins the group of his course and joins all groups for which the year of student's university entrance differs by no more than x from the year of university entrance of this student, where x — some non-negative integer. A value x is not given, but it can be uniquely determined from the available data. Note that students don't join other groups. You are given the list of groups which the student Igor joined. According to this information you need to determine the year of Igor's university entrance.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains the positive odd integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 5) — the number of groups which Igor joined.  The next line contains n distinct integers a1, a2, ..., an (2010 ≤ ai ≤ 2100) — years of student's university entrance for each group in which Igor is the member. It is guaranteed that the input data is correct and the answer always exists. Groups are given randomly.
problem_description.output_spec: Print the year of Igor's university entrance.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first test the value x = 1. Igor entered the university in 2015. So he joined groups members of which are students who entered the university in 2014, 2015 and 2016.In the second test the value x = 0. Igor entered only the group which corresponds to the year of his university entrance.

problem_description.description: There is the faculty of Computer Science in Berland. In the social net "TheContact!" for each course of this faculty there is the special group whose name equals the year of university entrance of corresponding course of students at the university. Each of students joins the group of his course and joins all groups for which the year of student's university entrance differs by no more than x from the year of university entrance of this student, where x — some non-negative integer. A value x is not given, but it can be uniquely determined from the available data. Note that students don't join other groups. You are given the list of groups which the student Igor joined. According to this information you need to determine the year of Igor's university entrance.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains the positive odd integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 5) — the number of groups which Igor joined.  The next line contains n distinct integers a1, a2, ..., an (2010 ≤ ai ≤ 2100) — years of student's university entrance for each group in which Igor is the member. It is guaranteed that the input data is correct and the answer always exists. Groups are given randomly.
problem_description.output_spec: Print the year of Igor's university entrance.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first test the value x = 1. Igor entered the university in 2015. So he joined groups members of which are students who entered the university in 2014, 2015 and 2016.In the second test the value x = 0. Igor entered only the group which corresponds to the year of his university entrance.

problem_description.description: While creating high loaded systems one should pay a special attention to caching. This problem will be about one of the most popular caching algorithms called LRU (Least Recently Used).Suppose the cache may store no more than k objects. At the beginning of the workflow the cache is empty. When some object is queried we check if it is present in the cache and move it here if it's not. If there are more than k objects in the cache after this, the least recently used one should be removed. In other words, we remove the object that has the smallest time of the last query.Consider there are n videos being stored on the server, all of the same size. Cache can store no more than k videos and caching algorithm described above is applied. We know that any time a user enters the server he pick the video i with probability pi. The choice of the video is independent to any events before.The goal of this problem is to count for each of the videos the probability it will be present in the cache after 10100 queries.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains two integers n and k (1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 20) — the number of videos and the size of the cache respectively. Next line contains n real numbers pi (0 ≤ pi ≤ 1), each of them is given with no more than two digits after decimal point. It's guaranteed that the sum of all pi is equal to 1.
problem_description.output_spec: Print n real numbers, the i-th of them should be equal to the probability that the i-th video will be present in the cache after 10100 queries. You answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed 10 - 6.  Namely: let's assume that your answer is a, and the answer of the jury is b. The checker program will consider your answer correct, if .

<your_rewritten_code_2>
#include <bits/stdc++.h>

using namespace std;

using ll = long long;
using ii = pair<int, int>;
using ld = long double;
using D = double;
using vi = vector<int>;
using vii = vector<ii>;
using vvi = vector<vi>;
using vs = vector<string>;

template<typename T> T my_abs(T x) { return x < 0 ? -x : x; }
template<typename T> int my_sgn(T x) { return x < 0 ? -1 : (x > 0 ? 1 : 0); }
template<typename T> T my_sqr(T x) { return x * x; }
template<typename T> T my_gcd(T a, T b) { return a ? my_gcd(b % a, a) : b; }

int main() {
    ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    int n, m;
    cin >> n >> m;
    
    vector<double> p(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cin >> p[i];
    
    vector<double> res(1 << n, 0.0);
    vector<double> q(n, 0.0);
    
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) res[1 << i] = p[i];
    
    for (int mask = 1; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {
        vector<int> included, excluded;
        double sum_excluded = 0.0;
        
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (mask & (1 << j)) {
                included.push_back(j);
            } else {
                excluded.push_back(j);
                sum_excluded += p[j];
            }
        }
        
        if (included.size() == m || (included.size() < m && sum_excluded < 1e-5)) {
            for (int idx : included) {
                q[idx] += res[mask];
            }
        } else if (included.size() < m) {
            for (int idx : excluded) {
                res[mask | (1 << idx)] += res[mask] * p[idx] / sum_excluded;
            }
        }
    }
    
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cout << fixed << setprecision(15) << q[i] << " ";
    cout << "\n";
    
    return 0;
}
</your_rewritten_code_2>

For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.input_spec: The input consists of two space-separated integers p and k (3 ≤ p ≤ 1 000 000, 0 ≤ k ≤ p - 1) on a single line. It is guaranteed that p is an odd prime number.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer, the number of distinct functions f modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first sample, p = 3 and k = 2. The following functions work:   f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.  f(0) = 0, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1.  f(0) = f(1) = f(2) = 0.

problem_description.description: As behooves any intelligent schoolboy, Kevin Sun is studying psycowlogy, cowculus, and cryptcowgraphy at the Bovinia State University (BGU) under Farmer Ivan. During his Mathematics of Olympiads (MoO) class, Kevin was confronted with a weird functional equation and needs your help. For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.input_spec: The input consists of two space-separated integers p and k (3 ≤ p ≤ 1 000 000, 0 ≤ k ≤ p - 1) on a single line. It is guaranteed that p is an odd prime number.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer, the number of distinct functions f modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first sample, p = 3 and k = 2. The following functions work:   f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.  f(0) = 0, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1.  f(0) = f(1) = f(2) = 0.

problem_description.description: As behooves any intelligent schoolboy, Kevin Sun is studying psycowlogy, cowculus, and cryptcowgraphy at the Bovinia State University (BGU) under Farmer Ivan. During his Mathematics of Olympiads (MoO) class, Kevin was confronted with a weird functional equation and needs your help. For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.input_spec: The input consists of two space-separated integers p and k (3 ≤ p ≤ 1 000 000, 0 ≤ k ≤ p - 1) on a single line. It is guaranteed that p is an odd prime number.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer, the number of distinct functions f modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first sample, p = 3 and k = 2. The following functions work:   f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.  f(0) = 0, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1.  f(0) = f(1) = f(2) = 0.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

constexpr int MAX_SIZE = 1000007;
constexpr int MOD = 1000000007;

int p, k;
bool seen[MAX_SIZE];
int freq[MAX_SIZE];
vector<int> lengths;

void explore(int start, int mult) {
    int cur = start;
    int len = 1;
    while ((1LL * mult * cur) % p != start) {
        cur = (1LL * mult * cur) % p;
        seen[cur] = true;
        ++len;
    }
    ++freq[len];
}

bool isNotPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return true;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) {
        if (n % i == 0) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

int main() {
    ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    cin >> p >> k;
    
    if (k == 0) {
        long long res = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < p - 1; ++i) {
            res = (res * p) % MOD;
        }
        cout << res << '\n';
        return 0;
    }
    
    for (int i = 0; i < p; ++i) {
        if (!seen[i]) {
            explore(i, k);
        }
    }
    
    for (int i = 1; i <= p; ++i) {
        if (freq[i]) lengths.push_back(i);
    }
    
    long long result = 1;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < lengths.size(); ++idx) {
        int L = lengths[idx];
        long long sum = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < lengths.size() && 1LL * lengths[j] * lengths[j] <= L; ++j) {
            int d = lengths[j];
            if (L % d == 0) {
                int q = L / d;
                sum = (sum + 1LL * d * freq[d]) % MOD;
                if (d != q) {
                    sum = (sum + 1LL * q * freq[q]) % MOD;
                }
            }
        }
        for (int rep = 0; rep < freq[L]; ++rep) {
            result = (result * sum) % MOD;
        }
    }
    
    cout << result << '\n';
    return 0;
}

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
const long long MOD = 1000000007;
long long fast_pow(long long base, long long exp) {
    long long res = 1;
    while (exp > 0) {
        if (exp & 1) res = (res * base) % MOD;
        base = (base * base) % MOD;
        exp /= 2;
    }
    return res;
}
int main() {
    long long p, k;
    cin >> p >> k;
    if (k == 0) {
        cout << fast_pow(p, p - 1);
    } else if (k == 1) {
        cout << fast_pow(p, p);
    } else {
        long long ord = 1;
        long long cur = k % p;
        while (cur != 1) {
            cur = (cur * k) % p;
            ord++;
            if (ord > p) break;
        }
        cout << fast_pow(p, (p - 1) / ord);
    }
    return 0;
}

const long long MOD = 1000000007;
long long power_mod(long long base, long long exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (long long i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result = (result * base) % MOD;
    }
    return result;
}

        long long current = k % p;
        while (current != 1) {
            current = (current * k) % p;
            order++;
        }
        cout << power_mod(p, (p - 1) / order);
    }
    return 0;
}

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

using i64 = long long;
using f80 = long double;

constexpr f80 PI = 3.141592654;
constexpr i64 MAX_SIZE = 1000500;
constexpr i64 MODULO = 1000000007;
constexpr i64 MAX_POW2 = 1000000000;

i64 cycle_counts[MAX_SIZE];
i64 visited[MAX_SIZE];
i64 divisor_sums[MAX_SIZE];

i64 find_cycle_length(i64 node, i64 factor, i64 modulus) {
    i64 length = 0;
    while (true) {
        if (visited[node]) break;
        visited[node] = 1;
        node = (node * factor) % modulus;
        ++length;
    }
    return length;
}

i64 fast_exp(i64 base, i64 exponent) {
    if (exponent == 0) return 1;
    i64 half_result = fast_exp(base, exponent / 2);
    if (exponent % 2 == 0) {
        return (half_result * half_result) % MODULO;
    } else {
        return (base * ((half_result * half_result) % MODULO)) % MODULO;
    }
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    i64 n, k;
    scanf("%lld %lld", &n, &k);

    if (k == 0) {
        printf("%lld\n", fast_exp(n, n - 1));
        return 0;
    }

    for (i64 i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (!visited[i]) {
            i64 len = find_cycle_length(i, k, n);
            cycle_counts[len]++;
        }
    }

    for (i64 d = 1; d <= n; ++d) {
        for (i64 m = d; m <= n; m += d) {
            if (cycle_counts[m]) {
                divisor_sums[m] += cycle_counts[d] * d;
            }
        }
    }

    i64 answer = 1;
    for (i64 d = 1; d <= n; ++d) {
        if (divisor_sums[d]) {
            answer = (answer * fast_exp(divisor_sums[d], cycle_counts[d])) % MODULO;
        }
    }

    printf("%lld\n", answer);
    return 0;
}
</your_rewritten_code_2>

problem_description.description: As behooves any intelligent schoolboy, Kevin Sun is studying psycowlogy, cowculus, and cryptcowgraphy at the Bovinia State University (BGU) under Farmer Ivan. During his Mathematics of Olympiads (MoO) class, Kevin was confronted with a weird functional equation and needs your help. For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.input_spec: The input consists of two space-separated integers p and k (3 ≤ p ≤ 1 000 000, 0 ≤ k ≤ p - 1) on a single line. It is guaranteed that p is an odd prime number.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer, the number of distinct functions f modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first sample, p = 3 and k = 2. The following functions work:   f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.  f(0) = 0, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1.  f(0) = f(1) = f(2) = 0.

For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1000000007;

int main() {
    int p, k;
    cin >> p >> k;

    if (k == 0) {
        long long ans = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < p; ++i) ans = (ans * p) % MOD;
        cout << ans;
        return 0;
    }

    if (k == 1) {
        long long ans = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < p; ++i) ans = (ans * p) % MOD;
        cout << ans;
        return 0;
    }

    vector<int> vis(p, 0);
    vector<long long> powMod(p + 1);
    powMod[0] = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i <= p; ++i) {
        powMod[i] = (powMod[i-1] * k) % p;
    }

    long long ans = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < p; ++i) {
        if (vis[i]) continue;
        int cur = i, len = 0;
        do {
            vis[cur] = 1;
            ++len;
            cur = (1LL * k * cur) % p;
        } while (!vis[cur]);
        if (powMod[len] == 1) {
            ans = (ans * p) % MOD;
        }
    }

    cout << ans;
    return 0;
}
</your_rewritten_code_2>

During his Mathematics of Olympiads (MoO) class, Kevin was confronted with a weird functional equation and needs your help. For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.input_spec: The input consists of two space-separated integers p and k (3 ≤ p ≤ 1 000 000, 0 ≤ k ≤ p - 1) on a single line. It is guaranteed that p is an odd prime number.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer, the number of distinct functions f modulo 109 + 7.
problem_description.notes: NoteIn the first sample, p = 3 and k = 2. The following functions work:   f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.  f(0) = 0, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1.  f(0) = f(1) = f(2) = 0.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
#include <ctime>

#pragma GCC target("sse,sse2,sse3,ssse3,sse4,popcnt,abm,mmx")

using namespace std;

using ll = long long;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
using vi = vector<int>;

const int MOD = 1000000007;
const int MAXN = 3000010;

int p, k, components;
bool visited[MAXN];

void traverse(int node) {
    visited[node] = true;
    int nextNode = (1LL * node * k) % p;
    if (!visited[nextNode]) {
        traverse(nextNode);
    }
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    cin >> p >> k;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < p; ++i) {
        if (!visited[i]) {
            components++;
            traverse(i);
        }
    }
    
    ll result = 1;
    int exponent = components + (k == 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < exponent; ++i) {
        result = (result * p) % MOD;
    }
    
    cout << result;
    
    return 0;
}

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
#include <ctime>

#pragma GCC target("sse,sse2,sse3,ssse3,sse4,popcnt,abm,mmx")

using namespace std;

using ll = long long;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
using vi = vector<int>;

const int MOD = 1000000007;
const int MAXN = 3000010;

int p, k, components;
bool visited[MAXN];

void traverse(int node) {
    visited[node] = true;
    int nextNode = (1LL * node * k) % p;
    if (!visited[nextNode]) {
        traverse(nextNode);
    }
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    cin >> p >> k;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < p; ++i) {
        if (!visited[i]) {
            components++;
            traverse(i);
        }
    }
    
    ll result = 1;
    int exponent = components + (k == 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < exponent; ++i) {
        result = (result * p) % MOD;
    }
    
    cout << result;
    
    return 0;
}

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
#include <ctime>

#pragma GCC target("sse,sse2,sse3,ssse3,sse4,popcnt,abm,mmx")

using namespace std;

using ll = long long;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
using vi = vector<int>;

const int MOD = 1000000007;
const int MAXN = 3000010;

int p, k, components;
bool visited[MAXN];

void traverse(int node) {
    visited[node] = true;
    int nextNode = (1LL * node * k) % p;
    if (!visited[nextNode]) {
        traverse(nextNode);
    }
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    cin >> p >> k;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < p; ++i) {
        if (!visited[i]) {
            components++;
            traverse(i);
        }
    }
    
    ll result = 1;
    int exponent = components + (k == 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < exponent; ++i) {
        result = (result * p) % MOD;
    }
    
    cout << result;
    
    return 0;
}

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
#include <ctime>

#pragma GCC target("sse,sse2,sse3,ssse3,sse4,popcnt,abm,mmx")

using namespace std;

using ll = long long;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
using vi = vector<int>;

const int MOD = 1000000007;
const int MAXN = 3000010;

int p, k, components;
bool visited[MAXN];

void traverse(int node) {
    visited[node] = true;
    int nextNode = (1LL * node * k) % p;
    if (!visited[nextNode]) {
        traverse(nextNode);
    }
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    cin >> p >> k;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < p; ++i) {
        if (!visited[i]) {
            components++;
            traverse(i);
        }
    }
    
    ll result = 1;
    int exponent = components + (k == 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < exponent; ++i) {
        result = (result * p) % MOD;
    }
    
    cout << result;
    
    return 0;
}

During his Mathematics of Olympiads (MoO) class, Kevin was confronted with a weird functional equation and needs your help. For two fixed integers k and p, where p is an odd prime number, the functional equation states that  for some function . (This equation should hold for any integer x in the range 0 to p - 1, inclusive.)It turns out that f can actually be many different functions. Instead of finding a solution, Kevin wants you to count the number of distinct functions f that satisfy this equation. Since the answer may be very large, you should print your result modulo 109 + 7.

problem_description.description: Everyone loves a freebie. Especially students.It is well-known that if in the night before exam a student opens window, opens the student's record-book and shouts loudly three times "Fly, freebie, fly!" — then flown freebie helps him to pass the upcoming exam.In the night before the exam on mathematical analysis n students living in dormitory shouted treasured words. The i-th student made a sacrament at the time ti, where ti is the number of seconds elapsed since the beginning of the night.It is known that the freebie is a capricious and willful lady. That night the freebie was near dormitory only for T seconds. Therefore, if for two students their sacrament times differ for more than T, then the freebie didn't visit at least one of them.Since all students are optimists, they really want to know what is the maximal number of students visited by the freebie can be.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 100), where n — the number of students shouted "Fly, freebie, fly!" The second line contains n positive integers ti (1 ≤ ti ≤ 1000). The last line contains integer T (1 ≤ T ≤ 1000) — the time interval during which the freebie was near the dormitory.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer — the largest number of people who will pass exam tomorrow because of the freebie visit.

problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer — the largest number of people who will pass exam tomorrow because of the freebie visit.

problem_description.description: Everyone loves a freebie. Especially students.It is well-known that if in the night before exam a student opens window, opens the student's record-book and shouts loudly three times "Fly, freebie, fly!" — then flown freebie helps him to pass the upcoming exam.In the night before the exam on mathematical analysis n students living in dormitory shouted treasured words. The i-th student made a sacrament at the time ti, where ti is the number of seconds elapsed since the beginning of the night.It is known that the freebie is a capricious and willful lady. That night the freebie was near dormitory only for T seconds. Therefore, if for two students their sacrament times differ for more than T, then the freebie didn't visit at least one of them.Since all students are optimists, they really want to know what is the maximal number of students visited by the freebie can be.

problem_description.description: Everyone loves a freebie. Especially students.It is well-known that if in the night before exam a student opens window, opens the student's record-book and shouts loudly three times "Fly, freebie, fly!" — then flown freebie helps him to pass the upcoming exam.In the night before the exam on mathematical analysis n students living in dormitory shouted treasured words. The i-th student made a sacrament at the time ti, where ti is the number of seconds elapsed since the beginning of the night.It is known that the freebie is a capricious and willful lady. That night the freebie was near dormitory only for T seconds. Therefore, if for two students their sacrament times differ for more than T, then the freebie didn't visit at least one of them.Since all students are optimists, they really want to know what is the maximal number of students visited by the freebie can be.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line of the input contains integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 100), where n — the number of students shouted "Fly, freebie, fly!" The second line contains n positive integers ti (1 ≤ ti ≤ 1000). The last line contains integer T (1 ≤ T ≤ 1000) — the time interval during which the freebie was near the dormitory.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single integer — the largest number of people who will pass exam tomorrow because of the freebie visit.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains two integers n and t (2 ≤ n ≤ 10, 1 ≤ t ≤ 60). Each of the next n lines contains n characters. These lines describe the scientists' locations. Then exactly one empty line follows. Each of the next n more lines contains n characters. These lines describe the rescue capsules' locations. In the description of the scientists' and the rescue capsules' locations the character "Y" stands for a properly functioning reactor, "Z" stands for the malfunctioning reactor. The reactors' positions in both descriptions coincide. There is exactly one malfunctioning reactor on the station. The digits "0" - "9" stand for the laboratories. In the description of the scientists' locations those numbers stand for the number of scientists in the corresponding laboratories. In the rescue capsules' descriptions they stand for the number of such capsules in each laboratory.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single number — the maximum number of scientists who will manage to save themselves.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains two integers n and t (2 ≤ n ≤ 10, 1 ≤ t ≤ 60). Each of the next n lines contains n characters. These lines describe the scientists' locations. Then exactly one empty line follows. Each of the next n more lines contains n characters. These lines describe the rescue capsules' locations. In the description of the scientists' and the rescue capsules' locations the character "Y" stands for a properly functioning reactor, "Z" stands for the malfunctioning reactor. The reactors' positions in both descriptions coincide. There is exactly one malfunctioning reactor on the station. The digits "0" - "9" stand for the laboratories. In the description of the scientists' locations those numbers stand for the number of scientists in the corresponding laboratories. In the rescue capsules' descriptions they stand for the number of such capsules in each laboratory.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single number — the maximum number of scientists who will manage to save themselves.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains two integers n and t (2 ≤ n ≤ 10, 1 ≤ t ≤ 60). Each of the next n lines contains n characters. These lines describe the scientists' locations. Then exactly one empty line follows. Each of the next n more lines contains n characters. These lines describe the rescue capsules' locations. In the description of the scientists' and the rescue capsules' locations the character "Y" stands for a properly functioning reactor, "Z" stands for the malfunctioning reactor. The reactors' positions in both descriptions coincide. There is exactly one malfunctioning reactor on the station. The digits "0" - "9" stand for the laboratories. In the description of the scientists' locations those numbers stand for the number of scientists in the corresponding laboratories. In the rescue capsules' descriptions they stand for the number of such capsules in each laboratory.
problem_description.output_spec: Print a single number — the maximum number of scientists who will manage to save themselves.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.

It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.

Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.

problem_description.description: They've screwed something up yet again... In one nuclear reactor of a research station an uncontrolled reaction is in progress and explosion which will destroy the whole station will happen soon.The station is represented by a square n × n divided into 1 × 1 blocks. Each block is either a reactor or a laboratory. There can be several reactors and exactly one of them will explode soon. The reactors can be considered impassable blocks, but one can move through laboratories. Between any two laboratories, which are in adjacent blocks, there is a corridor. Blocks are considered adjacent if they have a common edge.In each laboratory there is some number of scientists and some number of rescue capsules. Once the scientist climbs into a capsule, he is considered to be saved. Each capsule has room for not more than one scientist.The reactor, which is about to explode, is damaged and a toxic coolant trickles from it into the neighboring blocks. The block, which contains the reactor, is considered infected. Every minute the coolant spreads over the laboratories through corridors. If at some moment one of the blocks is infected, then the next minute all the neighboring laboratories also become infected. Once a lab is infected, all the scientists there that are not in rescue capsules die. The coolant does not spread through reactor blocks.There are exactly t minutes to the explosion. Any scientist in a minute can move down the corridor to the next lab, if it is not infected. On any corridor an unlimited number of scientists can simultaneously move in both directions. It is believed that the scientists inside a lab moves without consuming time. Moreover, any scientist could get into the rescue capsule instantly. It is also believed that any scientist at any given moment always has the time to perform their actions (move from the given laboratory into the next one, or climb into the rescue capsule) before the laboratory will be infected.Find the maximum number of scientists who will be able to escape.

#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>
#include <cmath>
#include <climits>
#include <cstdlib>
using namespace std;

using i64 = long long;

struct Fraction {
    i64 numerator;
    i64 denominator;
};

inline pair<i64, i64> computeApproximations(int x, int y, int b) {
    i64 num = static_cast<i64>(b) * x;
    i64 lower = num / y;
    i64 upper = (num + y - 1) / y;
    return {lower, upper};
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    int x, y, n;
    cin >> x >> y >> n;
    
    vector<Fraction> pool;
    pool.reserve(2 * n);
    
    for (int b = 1; b <= n; ++b) {
        auto [lo, hi] = computeApproximations(x, y, b);
        pool.push_back({lo, b});
        pool.push_back({hi, b});
    }
    
    auto distance = [&](i64 num, i64 den) -> i64 {
        return llabs(static_cast<i64>(x) * den - num * y);
    };
    
    auto cmp = [&](const Fraction& a, const Fraction& b) {
        i64 da = distance(a.numerator, a.denominator);
        i64 db = distance(b.numerator, b.denominator);
        if (da != db) return da < db;
        if (a.denominator != b.denominator) return a.denominator < b.denominator;
        return a.numerator < b.numerator;
    };
    
    nth_element(pool.begin(), pool.begin(), pool.end(), cmp);
    auto best = *min_element(pool.begin(), pool.end(), cmp);
    
    cout << best.numerator << "/" << best.denominator << '\n';
    
    return 0;
}
</your_rewritten_code_2>

    i64 lo = num / y;

    return {lo, hi};
}

#include <iostream>
#include <cmath>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    using LL = long long;
    LL x, y, n;
    cin >> x >> y >> n;

    LL bestRem = (1LL << 32);
    LL bestNum = (1LL << 32);
    LL bestDen = (1LL << 32);

    for (LL b = 1; b <= n; ++b) {
        LL baseA = (x * b) / y;
        if (baseA > 10) baseA -= 10;
        else baseA = 0;

        for (int j = 0; j < 20; ++j) {
            LL a = baseA + j;
            LL diff = llabs(x * b - a * y);
            
            if (bestRem * b > diff * bestDen) {
                bestRem = diff;
                bestNum = a;
                bestDen = b;
            } else if (bestRem * b == diff * bestDen) {
                if (bestDen > b || (bestDen == b && bestNum > a)) {
                    bestRem = diff;
                    bestNum = a;
                    bestDen = b;
                }
            }
        }
    }

    cout << bestNum << "/" << bestDen << endl;
    return 0;
}
</your_rewritten_code_1>

int main() {
    using int64 = long long;

    int64 x, y, n;

    int64 currentMinDiff = (int64)1 << 32;
    int64 bestA = (int64)1 << 32;
    int64 bestB = (int64)1 << 32;

    for (int64 b = 1; b <= n; ++b) {
        int64 aStart = (x * b) / y;
        aStart = max(aStart - 10LL, 0LL);

        for (int offset = 0; offset < 20; ++offset) {
            int64 aCandidate = aStart + offset;
            int64 diff = llabs(x * b - aCandidate * y);

            bool update = false;
            if (currentMinDiff * b > diff * bestB) {
                update = true;
            } else if (currentMinDiff * b == diff * bestB) {
                if (bestB > b || (bestB == b && bestA > aCandidate)) {
                    update = true;
                }
            }

            if (update) {
                currentMinDiff = diff;
                bestA = aCandidate;
                bestB = b;
            }
        }
    }

    cout << bestA << "/" << bestB << endl;
    return 0;
}

#include <tuple>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    using I64 = long long;

    I64 x, y, n;
    cin >> x >> y >> n;

    auto state = make_tuple(
        (I64)1 << 32,
        (I64)1 << 32,
        (I64)1 << 32
    );

    for (I64 b = 1; b <= n; ++b) {
        I64 baseA = (x * b) / y;
        baseA = max(baseA - 10, (I64)0);

        for (int k = 0; k < 20; ++k) {
            I64 a = baseA + k;
            I64 diff = llabs(x * b - a * y);

            auto& [rem, resA, resB] = state;
            bool shouldUpdate = false;

            if (rem * b > diff * resB) {
                shouldUpdate = true;
            } else if (rem * b == diff * resB) {
                if (resB > b || (resB == b && resA > a)) {
                    shouldUpdate = true;
                }
            }

            if (shouldUpdate) {
                rem = diff;
                resA = a;
                resB = b;
            }
        }
    }

    auto [rem, resA, resB] = state;
    cout << resA << "/" << resB << endl;
    return 0;
}

    using i64 = long long;
    i64 x, y, n;
    cin >> x >> y >> n;

    i64 res_a = i64(1) << 32;
    i64 res_b = i64(1) << 32;

    auto update_if_better = [&](i64 a, i64 b) {
        i64 diff = llabs(x * b - a * y);
        if (rem * b > diff * res_b) {
            rem = diff;
            res_a = a;
            res_b = b;
        } else if (rem * b == diff * res_b) {
            if (res_b > b || (res_b == b && res_a > a)) {
                rem = diff;
                res_a = a;
                res_b = b;
            }
        }
    };

    for (i64 b = 1; b <= n; ++b) {
        i64 a0 = x * b / y;
        if (a0 > 10) a0 -= 10;
        else a0 = 0;

        for (int j = 0; j < 20; ++j) {
            update_if_better(a0 + j, b);
        }
    }

    cout << res_a << "/" << res_b << endl;
    return 0;
}

problem_description.description: Integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ (inclusive) were sorted lexicographically (considering integers as strings). As a result, array $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ was obtained.Calculate value of $$$(\sum_{i = 1}^n ((i - a_i) \mod 998244353)) \mod 10^9 + 7$$$.$$$x \mod y$$$ here means the remainder after division $$$x$$$ by $$$y$$$. This remainder is always non-negative and doesn't exceed $$$y - 1$$$. For example, $$$5 \mod 3 = 2$$$, $$$(-1) \mod 6 = 5$$$.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains the single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 10^{12}$$$).
problem_description.output_spec: Print one integer — the required sum.
problem_description.notes: NoteA string $$$a$$$ is lexicographically smaller than a string $$$b$$$ if and only if one of the following holds:  $$$a$$$ is a prefix of $$$b$$$, but $$$a \ne b$$$;  in the first position where $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ differ, the string $$$a$$$ has a letter that appears earlier in the alphabet than the corresponding letter in $$$b$$$. For example, $$$42$$$ is lexicographically smaller than $$$6$$$, because they differ in the first digit, and $$$4 < 6$$$; $$$42 < 420$$$, because $$$42$$$ is a prefix of $$$420$$$.Let's denote $$$998244353$$$ as $$$M$$$.In the first example, array $$$a$$$ is equal to $$$[1, 2, 3]$$$.   $$$(1 - 1) \mod M = 0 \mod M = 0$$$  $$$(2 - 2) \mod M = 0 \mod M = 0$$$  $$$(3 - 3) \mod M = 0 \mod M = 0$$$ As a result, $$$(0 + 0 + 0) \mod 10^9 + 7 = 0$$$In the second example, array $$$a$$$ is equal to $$$[1, 10, 11, 12, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]$$$.   $$$(1 - 1) \mod M = 0 \mod M = 0$$$  $$$(2 - 10) \mod M = (-8) \mod M = 998244345$$$  $$$(3 - 11) \mod M = (-8) \mod M = 998244345$$$  $$$(4 - 12) \mod M = (-8) \mod M = 998244345$$$  $$$(5 - 2) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(6 - 3) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(7 - 4) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(8 - 5) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(9 - 6) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(10 - 7) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(11 - 8) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$  $$$(12 - 9) \mod M = 3 \mod M = 3$$$ As a result, $$$(0 + 998244345 + 998244345 + 998244345 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3) \mod 10^9 + 7$$$ $$$=$$$ $$$2994733059 \mod 10^9 + 7$$$ $$$=$$$ $$$994733045$$$

#include <cmath>

const long long MOD = 998244353LL;
const long long MODULO = 1000000007LL;
const int K_LEVELS = 7;
const long long BASE_VAL = 1000000LL;

long long n, counter;
int result;
long long prefix_sum[K_LEVELS];
vector<long long> sequences[K_LEVELS];

void traverse_first(long long num, int depth) {
    counter++;
    long long computed = ((counter - num) % MOD + MOD) % MOD;
    sequences[depth].push_back(computed);
    prefix_sum[depth] = (prefix_sum[depth] + computed) % MODULO;
    if (depth == 6) return;
    for (int d = 0; d <= 9; ++d) {
        traverse_first(num * 10 + d, depth + 1);
    }
}

void traverse_second(long long num) {
    if (num > n) return;
    if (num * BASE_VAL + BASE_VAL - 1 <= n && num * BASE_VAL * 10 > n) {
        long long current = counter;
        for (int level = 0, multiplier = 1; level <= 6; ++level, multiplier *= 10) {
            int size = sequences[level].size();
            long long diff = ((current - num * multiplier) % MOD + MOD) % MOD;
            int index = lower_bound(sequences[level].begin(), sequences[level].end(), MOD - diff) - sequences[level].begin();

    result = (result + (int)(((counter - num) % MOD + MOD) % MOD)) % MODULO;
    for (int d = 0; d <= 9; ++d) {
        traverse_second(num * 10 + d);
    }

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
typedef long long ll;
ll i, n, top, t, k, arr[500000], m = 2147483647LL, bs;

void f(ll x, ll s, ll k, ll kk) {
    if (s >= i) return;
    if (x == 0) {
        printf("%lld", s);
        exit(0);
    }
    while (k > x) { k /= 10; kk--; }
    f(0, s + ((k * 10 + 1) - x) + kk + 1, k * 10 + 1, kk + 1);
    ll t = x / k;
    f((k * 10 + 1) - x, s + kk + 1, k, kk);
    f(x - (k * t), s + (kk * t), k, kk);
}

int main() {
    scanf("%lld", &n);
    k = 1;
    bs = 1;
    while (k * 10 + 1 <= n) {
        k = k * 10 + 1;
        bs++;
    }
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        f(n, 0, k, bs);
    }
    if (m == 2147483647LL) m = min(n, 13 - n);
    printf("%lld", m);
}

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
#include <cmath>

using namespace std;

using i64 = long long;

i64 st[1000005];
i64 a[1000005];
i64 b[1000005];
i64 c[1000005];
i64 best = LLONG_MAX;

void evaluate() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 18; ++i) {
        a[i] = c[i];
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < 17; ++i) {
        if (b[i]) {
            a[i + 1]++;
            a[i] -= 10;
            a[0]--;
        }
    }
    if (a[0] < -6) {
        a[0] += 11;
        a[1]--;
    } else if (a[0] > 6) {
        a[0] -= 11;
        a[1]++;
    }
    i64 cost = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 18; ++i) {
        cost += abs(a[i]) * (i + 1);
    }
    best = min(best, cost);
}

void backtrack(int idx) {
    if (idx == 17) {
        evaluate();
        return;
    }
    for (int choice = 0; choice < 2; ++choice) {
        b[idx] = choice;
        backtrack(idx + 1);
    }
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    i64 n;
    cin >> n;
    st[0] = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < 18; ++i) {
        st[i] = st[i - 1] * 10 + 1;
    }
    i64 remaining = n;
    int index = 17;
    while (remaining > 0) {
        c[index] = remaining / st[index];
        remaining %= st[index];
        --index;
    }
    backtrack(0);
    cout << best;
}

problem_description.description: Sometimes one has to spell email addresses over the phone. Then one usually pronounces a dot as dot, an at sign as at. As a result, we get something like vasyaatgmaildotcom. Your task is to transform it into a proper email address (vasya@gmail.com). It is known that a proper email address contains only such symbols as . @ and lower-case Latin letters, doesn't start with and doesn't end with a dot. Also, a proper email address doesn't start with and doesn't end with an at sign. Moreover, an email address contains exactly one such symbol as @, yet may contain any number (possible, zero) of dots. You have to carry out a series of replacements so that the length of the result was as short as possible and it was a proper email address. If the lengths are equal, you should print the lexicographically minimal result. Overall, two variants of replacement are possible: dot can be replaced by a dot, at can be replaced by an at.
problem_description.input_spec: The first line contains the email address description. It is guaranteed that that is a proper email address with all the dots replaced by dot an the at signs replaced by at. The line is not empty and its length does not exceed 100 symbols.
problem_description.output_spec: Print the shortest email address, from which the given line could be made by the described above replacements. If there are several solutions to that problem, print the lexicographically minimal one (the lexicographical comparison of the lines are implemented with an operator < in modern programming languages). In the ASCII table the symbols go in this order: . @ ab...z

using namespace std;

int main() {
    string input, output;
    getline(cin, input);
    
    for (size_t i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) {
        if (i > 0 && input[i] == 'a' && input[i+1] == 't' && i + 2 < input.size() && 
            (i == 0 || input[i-1] != '@')) {
            output += '@';
            ++i;
        } else if (i + 2 < input.size() && input[i] == 'd' && input[i+1] == 'o' && input[i+2] == 't') {
            output += '.';
            i += 2;
        } else {
            output += input[i];
        }
    }
    
    cout << output << endl;
    return 0;
}

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int main() {
    string line;
    getline(cin, line);
    
    vector<char> chars(line.begin(), line.end());
    vector<char> result;
    bool at_replaced = false;
    
    for (size_t i = 0; i < chars.size(); ++i) {
        if (i > 0 && !at_replaced && chars[i] == 'a' && chars[i+1] == 't' && i + 2 < chars.size()) {
            result.push_back('@');
            ++i;
            at_replaced = true;
        } else if (chars[i] == 'd' && i + 2 < chars.size() && chars[i+1] == 'o' && chars[i+2] == 't') {
            result.push_back('.');
            i += 2;
        } else {
            result.push_back(chars[i]);
        }
    }
    
    for (char c : result) {
        cout << c;
    }
    cout << endl;
    
    return 0;
}
</your_rewritten_code_3>

    string input, output;
    getline(cin, input);
    
    size_t i = 0;
    while (i < input.size()) {
        if (i > 0 && input[i] == 'a' && i + 1 < input.size() && input[i+1] == 't' && i + 2 < input.size() && 
            find(input.begin(), input.begin() + i, '@') == input.begin() + i) {
            output += '@';
            i += 2;

            output += '.';

            output += input[i];
            i++;
        }
    }
    
    cout << output << endl;
    return 0;
}

#include <string>
#include <regex>

using namespace std;

int main() {
    string input, output;
    getline(cin, input);
    
    regex at_pattern("([^.@].*)@at(.*)");
    regex dot_pattern("([^.@].*)\\.dot(.*)");
    
    string temp = regex_replace(input, regex("at(?=[^.]|$)"), "@");
    while (temp.find("at") != string::npos) {
        size_t pos = temp.find("at");
        if (pos > 0 && temp[pos-1] != '.' && temp[pos-1] != '@' && pos + 2 < temp.size()) {
            temp = temp.substr(0, pos-1) + "@" + temp.substr(pos+2);
        } else {
            break;
        }
    }
    
    temp = regex_replace(temp, regex("dot"), ".");
    
    cout << temp << endl;
    return 0;
}

problem_description.description: This is an easier version of the problem. In this version, $$$n \le 6$$$.Marek is working hard on creating strong testcases to his new algorithmic problem. You want to know what it is? Nah, we're not telling you. However, we can tell you how he generates the testcases.Marek chooses an integer $$$n$$$ and $$$n^2$$$ integers $$$p_{ij}$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$, $$$1 \le j \le n$$$). He then generates a random bipartite graph with $$$2n$$$ vertices. There are $$$n$$$ vertices on the left side: $$$\ell_1, \ell_2, \dots, \ell_n$$$, and $$$n$$$ vertices on the right side: $$$r_1, r_2, \dots, r_n$$$. For each $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$, he puts an edge between vertices $$$\ell_i$$$ and $$$r_j$$$ with probability $$$p_{ij}$$$ percent.It turns out that the tests will be strong only if a perfect matching exists in the generated graph.
